title: AI Process Analysis and Automation Design

questions.question: Why should AI automation start with process analysis?
options: Because process maps are never useful once a team has decided to automate
Because AI automation removes every exception a manual process used to handle
Because automation can make an unclear process faster but less reliable
Because a human fallback plan is never needed once automation is running
questions.explanation: The lesson starts with process understanding because automating an unclear process just makes it faster and less reliable — process maps stay useful, AI doesn't remove exceptions, and a human fallback is still needed.

questions.question: Every invoice above a certain amount has to be manually re-typed from a PDF into three separate systems before anyone can approve it. Which of the lesson's four signals does this match most directly?
options: Process pain — the workflow is slow or frustrating, without pointing to one specific cause
Manual handoff — the same information is retyped by hand between systems or people
Exception volume — the workflow has to branch into unusual cases that are hard to plan for
Automation risk — automating this step could plausibly cause real, hard-to-reverse harm
questions.explanation: Re-typing the same invoice data by hand into three systems is the lesson's manual-handoff signal — distinct from general process pain, exception volume (branching edge cases), or automation risk (harm from automating).

questions.question: What does the Python artifact produce?
options: A finished workflow engine that can be deployed to production without a pilot test run
A process map that stays hidden from the team until automation is complete
A physical robot configured to perform the manual handoff automatically
A ranked automation triage plan with controls and rationale for each scenario
questions.explanation: The artifact ranks process scenarios into an automation triage plan with controls and rationale — it doesn't ship a workflow engine, hide the process map, or produce physical automation.

questions.question: Which control belongs to this lesson?
options: Skipping exception logging because most cases are expected to be routine, before defining the measurement, acceptance threshold, or rollback path
Removing the process owner once the automation pilot has been approved
Hiding the value check so the pilot can start before impact is estimated
Human fallback — a person who can step in whenever automation hits an exception
questions.explanation: The lesson's controls are process map, value check, exception log, and human fallback — human fallback keeps a person able to step in on exceptions, unlike skipping exception logs, removing the owner, or hiding the value check.

questions.question: When should an automation idea receive stronger review?
options: When exception volume, automation risk, or manual handoffs are present
Only when the process has already been automated and is running in production
Only when the process has no measurable value to the business at all
Never — a convincing tool demo is enough evidence to greenlight automation
questions.explanation: High exception volume, automation risk, manual handoffs, or high value potential are exactly the signals that call for stronger review — not an already-automated process, zero measured value, or a demo standing in for review.

questions.question: What should teams know before piloting AI automation?
options: Only the name of the model that will power the automated workflow
Only the length of the prompt used to drive the automated workflow, with no need to inspect intermediate results or test edge cases
The process map, value check, exception log, and human fallback plan
No details about the current manual process before automating it
questions.explanation: Before piloting, teams need the process map, a value check, an exception log, and a fallback plan — not just a model name, a prompt length, or no knowledge of the current process.
